abouts: context window truncation in contract review
subject: context window overflow degrades LLM output
agree: Exceeding an LLM's context window produces failures that stay invisible until they've already done damage: a legal memo silently drops the last 60% of a contract with 'no signal to the reviewing lawyer,' an orchestration pipeline's cost stays 'unmetered until production scale' before spiking to $50K/month, and an agent's reasoning 'shows no visible symptoms until reasoning quality collapses' after 20-30 iterations — three independently authored sources (the claude-for-legal plugin set, Titan, and context-fundamentals) each land on the same shape of failure: silent until it isn't.

read_first.why: The quote gives only the symptom (70-80% window consumption, no visible signs) — the source itself covers the attention mechanics that explain why quality degrades before quantity runs out, which is the causal mechanism the legal and Titan quotes only show the downstream damage from.

subject: LLM-as-judge evaluation reliability and fragility
agree: Judge outputs are sensitive to surface-level prompt and pipeline details — reasoning-vs-verdict ordering and minor wording changes both produce material score swings (02-metric-design's CoT-then-Score AUC gap, advanced-evaluation's wording-sensitivity claim)

Trusting a single judge run is unsafe — both implement-task (reject suspicious 5.0/5.0 scores) and the research-paper-writing incident (panel degraded from 3 to 2 judges silently blocked convergence for 11+ passes) show that judge setups need active scrutiny or redundancy, not blind acceptance of output

read_first.why: The quote gives only the outcome (2 judges → no convergence, 3 judges → 2 passes); the source will show how the broken Gemini parser was diagnosed, what convergence criteria and quorum the panel actually enforces, and how 'incumbent' scoring works — the mechanics needed to replicate or defend against this failure mode, which the same quote also appears verbatim in NousResearch/hermes-agent's copy of this skill, so either source carries it, but this one is worth opening first to see the full panel-convergence logic.

why_not: The shared word is "extraction," but it covers two unrelated subjects. Four of the six claims (materials-science, engineering, hydrology, and climate-ecology reviewer skills, all from the same GeoGeekLab/nature-reviewer-skills repo) share one identical, verbatim boilerplate sentence telling a peer reviewer to disclose when document extraction dropped figures/tables/equations — that's copy-pasted instruction text within one author's sibling skills, not independent agreement. The other two (HKUDS pdf-extraction-fallbacks and aipoch arxiv-preflight) are about a different subject entirely: the technical reliability of PDF/document text extraction itself (timeouts for corrupted files, preferring LaTeX source over PDF parsing).
agree: PDF/document text extraction is unreliable and needs explicit safeguards or workarounds — HKUDS's skill handles this by setting timeouts because 'PDF processing can hang on corrupted files,' while aipoch's skill handles it by avoiding PDF parsing altogether, preferring LaTeX source because 'PDF text extraction loses structure and produces noisier reference checks.'

read_first.why: The quoted timeout line is one item in a larger fallback strategy — the skill itself lays out the sequential extraction methods, failure detection, diagnostic logging, and cleanup steps that make PDF extraction robust, which the single sentence doesn't convey on its own.

why_not: They share only the phrase 'false positive(s)', not a subject. The five claims belong to unrelated domains: cloud-saas-exposure (severity-gating cloud bucket/storage findings), hla-typing (a clinical genotyping miscall risking a wrongly denied abacavir therapy), email-domain-security (crying subdomain/domain takeover on a transient DNS hiccup), ab-test-setup (statistical peeking inflating false-positive rates in A/B tests), and NousResearch/hermes-agent's desktop app (a connection test that passes on HTTP but misses a failed WebSocket/auth leg).

abouts: automated accessibility gates missing visual bugs
subject: automated a11y gates miss visible UI bugs
agree: Passing automated accessibility checks (contrast checkers, axe) does not mean the UI actually works — plugin87's design-system and design-component skills independently list the same concrete failure modes (a checkbox that won't toggle, a dash sitting at the bottom of its box, mismatched checkmark/dash stroke weight), and design-code states the conclusion directly: 'Gates don't catch this — you must.'

Automated scanners have a hard coverage ceiling that manual review must fill: Uxcel-Lab quantifies it at ~30-40% of issues caught, leaving focus order, alt-text quality, and reading order to human inspection, while the plugin87 skills reach the same conclusion from the component-defect side rather than the WCAG-criterion side.

read_first.why: The quote lists the symptoms gates miss but not the fix; the source defines the rendering-harness verification step that actually catches toggle/animation/weight defects before a component spec is considered done.

abouts: task completion verification via tool output
subject: Premature agent task-completion detection
agree: Surface signals of being done — assistant prose, a passing test, an opened PR, a finished plan, a trivial edit — are not reliable evidence of actual completion.

Agents default toward declaring work finished prematurely unless completion is checked against something durable (tool results, files, an explicit terminal state) rather than the agent's own narration.

read_first.why: The quote gives only the measured effect (~4x lower premature-completion rate). The source spells out the actual enforcement mechanism behind that number: verifying the most recently completed feature end-to-end before starting new work, and reverting/reopening/fixing that feature alone if verification fails — the concrete protocol the other three claims gesture at but don't specify.

why_not: The shared word is "completion" (completion rate / completed the operation), but it covers two unrelated subjects: (1) the retro-enforcement and meeting-notes claims are both about completion RATES of human-owned action items (tracked as GitHub issues vs. markdown, or with owner+date vs. without); (2) the two computer-use claims are both about NOT mistaking input dispatch for actual task completion during GUI automation. These are different domains — one is a workflow/accountability metric, the other is a technical verification rule for automated actions — that happen to share a root word.

abouts: stratified sample size and confidence interval
subject: minimum sample size for reliable estimates
agree: Naive assumptions about how much data is needed run wildly low: ab-test-plan shows the absolute-vs-relative reading error alone inflates required N by ~200x, and light-research-plan shows a commonly-used n=5/group carries only 10.8% power where 64/group is needed for 0.8 — both independently establish that intuitive sample sizes are off by an order of magnitude or more.

When N falls below a minimum threshold, the right move is to withhold or flag the derived statistic rather than report it as trustworthy: skill-cost-projections skips the projection outright below 2 data points, and eval-design only treats coverage as adequate at 30+ per stratum, tying smaller N explicitly to an unreliably wide CI (~±9%).

read_first.why: The quote gives one power-analysis output (n=5 vs n=64), but the source holds the full pipeline that produces it — the failure tree, effect-size assumptions, and preregistration gate that force a design to justify its N before it's allowed through, which is the general machinery the other three skills' thresholds (2 steps, 30/stratum, absolute-vs-relative sample size) are each a narrower instance of.

subject: false privilege markings on DPIAs
agree: Marking a document "ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT" does not itself create privilege protection, and asserting it where it doesn't hold is worse than making no privilege claim at all
The specific failure case cited is a DPIA reviewed by a data protection authority, where a false work-product assertion undermines the lawyer's position rather than shielding it

read_first.why: This is the one whose stated scope is privacy audits and DPIA production, so its full guardrails handbook should spell out what actually does confer privilege on a DPIA (versus the false marking this quote warns against) and how the plugin structures that analysis to avoid the failure mode — context the one-line warning alone doesn't give. Note the sentence is copied verbatim across all three sibling plugins in the claude-for-legal suite, so its presence in three skills reflects one shared boilerplate warning, not three independently-reached conclusions.

subject: concurrent writers silently clobber shared state files
agree: When two processes read the same file, edit it independently, and write back the whole thing, the last write wins and the other writer's changes vanish with no error
Downstream consumers treat the clobbered file as a normal, valid edit — there is no signal that data was lost, so the failure surfaces later or not at all

read_first.why: The other two only diagnose the race; this one is the fix. Its quote is a compressed protocol ('re-read immediately before writing... reclassify rather than overwrite') — the source will spell out how to detect that a term changed underneath you and merge instead of blindly overwriting, which is the missing half of the other two skills' problem statements.

why_not: The claims share the word "bias" (self-rating bias, LLM-pairing bias, training-prior bias) but describe three unrelated subjects: agent-evaluation methodology (judges rating outputs), an ideation engine's use of randomness to avoid biased pairings, and a Chinese video-script-writing assistant countering the model's format default.

read_first.why: Of the three, this is the only skill whose claim describes an evaluation-methodology finding (LLM self-preference bias) with likely follow-through — the source would show the rubric/test-set design used to detect and correct for that bias, which the single sentence alone doesn't convey.

subject: Post-it note length limit convention
agree: Post-it notes in this multi-skill system (My-Brain-Is-Full-Crew) are capped at 30 lines and must be summarized rather than allowed to grow into a journal
The same length constraint is enforced identically across unrelated skill types (audio transcription and email triage), showing it is a shared system-wide convention rather than a per-skill rule

read_first.why: The quote is just the post-it size rule; the source shows the full post-it template and mode-specific structure (meeting/lecture/podcast/interview/journal) plus the intake interview that decides what gets condensed into those 30 lines, and is the canonical skill file rather than the tests/regression/snapshot copy duplicated alongside it.

subject: verify actual working directory before file ops
agree: An operation that writes or moves files must use the actual current working directory rather than an assumed one (e.g. the skill's own directory), or output ends up in the wrong place.
The failure is common enough that skills bake in an explicit directory check as a first step rather than trusting a default.

read_first.why: The quote is one row of a larger failure-scenario-to-mitigation table; the source shows the full set of pre-flight checks (of which 'run pwd first' is just one) and why this planning skill treats state-verification as a gate before any implementation step, giving the general principle behind the narrower nano-banana-pro fix.

why_not: The shared word is "file": two claims (deeplake-memory and hivemind-memory, both from activeloopai/hivemind, duplicated across the codex and claude-code harnesses) are about skipping a memory file that returns empty after retries, while the third (filesystem-context) is about checking file size before reading to avoid flooding the context window — these are not the same subject, just two skills that both happen to mention 'a file.'

read_first.why: This is the one claim in the group not duplicated elsewhere, and its summary points to concrete patterns for persisting large tool outputs to disk instead of the token budget — the quote only states the failure mode (100K+ tokens dumped from an unchecked read), not the size thresholds or storage pattern the skill actually prescribes to avoid it.

subject: landing page design for conversion
agree: Attention on a landing page is scarce and largely unread, so design must impose hierarchy and prioritization rather than treating all copy or sections as equally weighted — supported independently by the tinte-design claim (a page of equal-weight sections 'has no argument') and the Uxcel claim (users form an impression in ~0.05s and read as little as ~20% of the copy).

read_first.why: The quoted 7%-per-field statistic is one line from a full seven-section CRO framework — the source holds the actual audit checklist (copy, form, mobile, speed), scoring rubric, and prioritized-fix methodology needed to apply that number to a real page, not just the number itself.

subject: geometric proxy checks miss real failures
agree: A fast geometric or staged check (bounding-box overlap, a passing test suite) can report success while the actual rendered, perceptual, or real-environment result is still broken.

The gap between the proxy and the real object matters most at edge cases the proxy can't see: hollow/complex geometry for AABB collision, low-contrast or overlapping elements for a bbox label check, and large real-layout gaps for a staged drag-and-drop test.

read_first.why: The quote states the warning, but the source supplies the explicit numeric acceptance criteria and bundled smoke-test script that operationalize it — telling you exactly when a bounding-box collision is trustworthy versus when hollow frames, windows, handles, or side plates require checking the rendered mesh instead.

subject: variance thresholds separate real signal from noise
agree: An observed change (a performance gain, a benchmark score, a rerun's metric) cannot be judged real until it is compared against the natural variance of repeated measurement — inside that band, the difference is not an effect, it's sampling noise.
Insufficient repetition or sample size is what produces that misleading noise band in the first place, whether from too few benchmark runs or too few identical-seed reruns.

read_first.why: The quote gives one worked example (±0.15 mAP across node counts); the source holds the full variance-reporting template and recipe ledger that generalizes this into a reusable disclosure format — compute conditions, determinism notes, and per-row variance bounds — so a reader can apply the same bug-vs-physics test to their own results rather than just this one benchmark row.

subject: ARIA live region announcement reliability
agree: To make a live region announce the same message twice, the region's content must actually change after load — clearing or resetting it before writing the new text is what triggers the announcement, not just the same text being present again.

read_first.why: The quote gives the pattern (stable empty region, updated in place) but not the caveat it flags in the same breath — that dynamically inserted alert nodes behave inconsistently across screen readers. The source should carry the actual test matrix or code pattern for which screen readers were checked and how, which the one-line claim only gestures at.

abouts: tool failure handling in plan review
subject: isolating process failure from real output
agree: A failure in the automated/review step (rate limit, tool crash, one agent in a batch) must not be allowed to corrupt or replace the genuine output — the schematics skill keeps the generated image and invents no score, the plan-reviewer keeps tool failure out of the domain-finding pool, and the testing-handbook generator keeps the other agents' completed work rather than discarding the whole batch.

None of the three treats a failure as grounds for wholesale rejection: each narrows the blast radius to just the failed unit (one image's score, one finding's confidence, one agent's task) instead of invalidating everything around it.

read_first.why: The quote gives the rule (tool failure ≠ domain finding, block only when evidence is missing) but not the mechanics — the source spells out the confidence-tiering rubric and the exact evidence thresholds that decide when reduced confidence is merely noted versus when it's serious enough to block, which is the reusable part for building other read-only review skills.

subject: numeric stop-rules for diminishing returns
agree: Each skill converts 'diminishing returns' into a concrete number rather than leaving it to judgment: 85%/1-point/3-round for paper refinement, a 25-page cap for brand-voice sampling, a two-turn no-delta rule for sub-agent delegation.

Two of the three (content-refinement-agent and agent-team-dev) specifically ground the stop condition in a *streak* of non-improvement — 3 consecutive rounds under 1 point, two consecutive turns with no actionable delta — rather than a single bad round triggering a halt.

read_first.why: The quote gives only the plateau number; the source shows the scoring rubric, snapshot/revert mechanism, and critique memory that generate that 85%/1-point figure, which is the part a reader would need to reuse the rule rather than just cite it.

subject: AI hallucination demands source verification
agree: AI-generated synthesis of source material (citations, statistics, or quoted speech) fabricates content at a rate high enough that it cannot be trusted without checking it against the original source
This isn't a vague worry — it gets treated as reason to build an explicit verification step into the workflow rather than trusting the model's output on faith

read_first.why: The quote only cites Teresa Torres's 30% figure as motivation; the source will show the actual mechanism this skill built in response — how it checks each quoted line in the output snapshot against the source transcript before the document is delivered, which is the concrete safeguard the statistic is used to justify.

subject: the lost-in-the-middle context effect
agree: Long-context LLM retrieval is not uniform: information placed at the start or end of the context is recalled reliably, while the same information placed in the middle degrades — a pattern all three sources independently name as "lost in the middle."

read_first.why: The other two cite the effect to justify a narrower practice (CLAUDE.md structuring, system-prompt density); this one builds a full response to it — budgeting, retrieval, compaction, memory, tool-result pruning, and progressive disclosure — so it's where you'd find what to actually do about the effect, not just evidence that it exists.

why_not: The shared word is "path" — but it names two unrelated things. The qmd claim is about a cache-key value doubling as a sqlite filesystem path (`~/.cache/qmd/<name>.sqlite`) and needing validation before use, which belongs to Obsidian-vault search indexing, not CLI installation. The cli-creator and printing-press-rich-auth claims are both about validating an installed CLI binary from outside its source tree and on $PATH — a real, shared subject that the qmd claim has nothing to do with.
agree: cli-creator and printing-press-rich-auth independently establish that a CLI's installation isn't verified until it's run from outside the source/build directory — cli-creator by smoke-testing from /tmp, printing-press-rich-auth by treating a post-install "command not found" as diagnostic of the binary directory being missing from $PATH.

read_first.why: It's the actual skill guide (runtime selection, auth/JSON/safety contracts, installation, smoke testing) rather than a golden test fixture — reading it shows the full installation/smoke-test procedure the quoted line is one step of, whereas the printing-press-rich-auth source is testdata/golden/expected output demonstrating one generated CLI's docs, not the general procedure itself.
